title: Kisa Gotami's song
hook: her own verses: good friends, grief, and the deathless found (Therigatha, Kisa Gotami)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahapajapati sang her thanks to the one she raised. Your line was thanks to the child. Today, a woman known for one story, singing about something else.

Friends come first. That's where Kisa Gotami's own song begins, before any grief. The path met her before in the commentaries' story: the dead child carried from door to door, the mustard seed from a house where no one has died, every house with its dead. That story belongs to the commentaries. In the Therigatha, in her own verses, she puts something else ahead of it.
screen: `FRIENDS COME FIRST.` → `THE MUSTARD SEED: A COMMENTARY STORY.` → `HER OWN SONG, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. Good friendship, she says, has been praised by the Sage. Keep company with good friends, and even a fool would grow wise. Stay close to good people; that's how wisdom grows, and in their company one is freed from every suffering. She puts this before anything else. Second, the grief. Her verses do hold terrible loss: a woman on the road, giving birth far from home, a husband found dead, children gone, a family burned on one pyre. The commentary connects these lines with Patacara; some readers hear them as Kisa Gotami's own. Either way, the song doesn't look away. It speaks of tears shed across countless lives. Third, the turn. Bereaved, she says, looked down on, I reached the deathless. I have walked the noble eightfold path. I have seen nibbana. I have looked into the mirror of the teaching. The arrow is cut out, the burden is set down. Fourth, the shape: friends first, then grief, then freedom. Read in that order, the friends aren't decoration. Even in the mustard-seed story she isn't alone: she knocks on door after door, and every household tells her the truth, someone has died here too. The suttas have a word for this, good friendship, and when Ananda calls it half of the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: it's the whole of it. Kisa Gotami's song seems to agree.
screen: `GOOD FRIENDS, PRAISED FIRST.` · `THE ROAD, THE PYRE, THE TEARS.` · `I HAVE SEEN THE DEATHLESS.` · `FRIENDS, THEN GRIEF, THEN FREEDOM.` · then, large: `GOOD FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a friend who stayed when things were hard, or told you a true thing kindly, and remember one moment with them: what they said, where you were, what the light was like. Then simply wish them well. If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if you don't, hold them in your attention, the way you'd keep a hand on a friend's shoulder.
Kalyanamitta. A good friend, a friend in the good: friends first in Kisa Gotami's song, then grief, then the deathless found. Today's word.
Your line: good friends. Friends first, then grief, then freedom, in that order. Day seven hundred ninety, done.

howItsDone: Some Theravada teachers tell Kisa Gotami's mustard-seed story when they speak about death and grief, and return to good friendship when they speak of walking the path with others.

chat.says: Isn't Kisa Gotami's story mostly about grief?
options: Her own song puts good friends first, then grief, then the deathless found.
Yes. Her song is only about the mustard seed and her son.
No. Her song says she never grieved at all, once she was a nun.
chat.meaning: In the Therigatha, Kisa Gotami opens with good friendship, then tells of grief, then says she reached the deathless. The mustard seed belongs to the commentaries.

Kisa Gotami.meaning: the mother of the mustard-seed story, later a nun

Kalyanamitta.meaning: a good friend, a friend in the good

Therigatha.meaning: the verses of the elder nuns, in the Pali canon

nibbana.meaning: a flame going out; the goal of the whole path
